HEADLINE: Optimism and caution
TEXT:
Media CEOs on the themes for 2022

Cathy O’Connor oOH!Media CEO  Social platforms should be made to operate on a level playing field with other forms of media.

They are publishers as much as they are platforms and so should be subject to tighter regulation.

We need a regulatory framework that provides users of social platforms with protections against fake news and more transparency around the use of their data.

Mike Sneesby Nine Entertainment CEO  The media bargaining code has been an important step in helping to ensure that local media companies are fairly compensated for the journalism and content they produce. Furthermore, the code sends a clear message to global platforms that operating in Australia comes with the obligation to operate fairly.

James Warburton Seven West Media CEO and managing director  The government’s recent move to make social media companies responsible for posts made on their platforms is undoubtedly an important step forward, and they should be applauded for that. But the key strategy for combating disinformation remains ensuring that trusted news sources are widely and freely available to all Australians.

Will Easton Meta Australia and NZ managing director  Since the beginning of the pandemic, Facebook has taken aggressive steps to combat harmful COVID-19 misinformation and will continue to work with health experts to make sure that our approach and our policies are in the right place as required.

Jane Huxley Are Media CEO  The bargaining code has been a bit disappointing for smaller publishers and more needs to be done to ensure they are not sidelined by the social media giants. The behaviour has not really been in the spirit of the media bargaining code so far and has unfortunately created an even more uneven playing field.

Michael Miller News Corp Australasia executive chairman  I do feel that there will be more consolidation in the media.

Not all will survive, that’s my thesis. Some will need to change their business models, change their content offering and be more focused on different audience groups.

Beverley McGarvey ViacomCBS Australia and NZ executive vicepresident  What the 2020 bushfires, the COVID-19 pandemic and the recent floods have shown is that Australians turn to trusted and reliable Australian news media, particularly free-to-air television, when they require credible information. We are hopeful that governments will do all they can to protect this critical public service.

Patrick Delany Foxtel CEO  Our traditional, pay-TV business, Foxtel, is still subjected to company-specific heavy regulation where there is aggressive unregulated competition from scaled global and local players. In Australia, global streamers operate without any regulation, and local free TV now combines with the subscription streaming subsidiaries to make regulation redundant.

Jason Pellegrino Domain CEO  Consolidation feels like an analogue solution to a digital problem.Consolidation alone doesn’t help media organisations to be in a better position to help that discussion, and in fact, it might be a distraction.

Steve O’Connor JCDecaux CEO  Once there’s more stability in some media sectors, there could be more consolidation in 2023. There’ll be a lot of tyre kicking next year

HEADLINE: the 'bug out' property phenomenon
TEXT:
There’s now a crossover between rental and owner-occupied property as investors look for retreats and ‘workstations’.

Investors in residential property will increasingly buy rental homes and opt to live there themselves for periods over 2022, many experts believe.

The new phenomenon of having a “bug-out” place – somewhere to retreat to in the case of emergencies, such as lockdowns – is likely to be uppermost in most investors’ minds next year.

“What we have discovered is that a quarter of people are now living in their property before they rent it out as an investment,” says Mike Mortlock, director of MCG Quantity Surveying.

“This is so interesting as ... even though property advisors would say this is a poor investment strategy, this is happening more and more. People like to have a spread of options so they can disappear to somewhere else, like an investment property, if something goes wrong.”

The national director of group risk and compliance at valuers Herron Todd White, Kevin Brogan, predicts this new phenomenon will continue through next year.

“We’re seeing this crossover between rental property and owner-occupied property,” he says.

“People are buying investments, and then choosing to live there for two to three months – perhaps in a more conducive environment than their own homes [or] closer to their work – as a “workstation”, and then rent them out the rest of the year. The nexus between work and the office has been broken to a degree and now we’re seeing dual-purpose homes that the owners can use but also rent out.”

Property prices will continue to rise in 2022, but not at the same rate as this year, most predict. Although no one yet knows the extent of the macro-prudential tightening on lending that will take place, and how soon the Reserve Bank might raise interest rates, there’s still plenty of fat built into the system to allow most investors peace of mind.

“We haven’t had an interest rate rise now for 11 years,” says Peter Koulizos, chair of Property Investment Professionals of Australia. “But if the banks are comfortable with rates rising, then we should be too.

“Australian residential property is very resilient, which you can’t say of some commercial property. But we will see a continued movement away from Sydney and Melbourne to cities like Adelaide, Hobart and Brisbane, and to the regions.”

Brisbane is also a favourite pick for 2022 for Mortlock. “There’s still an affordability price point there and people have been saying for 10 years that Brisbane will be the next to boom because the salary-to-price ratio is good. But it never happened. [It] could happen in 2022, though, as another aspirational bug-out plan.”

Investors are likely to feel more comfortable about buying properties outside Sydney and Melbourne as tenants, too, take a postpandemic look at their lifestyles, and feel happier living out of inner cities or in regional and coastal locations.

“People now have a different lens on location, location, location,” says Brogan. “They’re now looking for different things in a home, and are willing to live further out for the sake of more space to work from home.”

HEADLINE: Queensland coast is pure gold
TEXT:
Buyers have been converging on the Gold Coast’s luxury properties like moths to a flame – with spectacular results.

By SARAH WEBB

Two years ago, prestige property prices across the Gold Coast were all but becalmed on a stagnant sea that left luxury mansions sitting like flotsam and jetsam in the real estate listings following a decade of static growth.

But just when it felt like the city’s gleam could fade, the perfect storm of COVID-19 and low interest rates propelled luxury home prices to unprecedented heights to cement a year of record-breaking growth that saw Surfers Paradise and Southport named two of the country’s top-selling suburbs.

Fuelled by a mammoth sea-change trend, home prices in sought-after pockets across the “glitter strip” rose by up to 44 per cent and shot 11 suburbs into the million-dollar-median club – a club that, 12 months earlier, had consisted of just Mermaid Beach and Surfers Paradise.

The figures, lifted from the Domain House Price Report for September 2021, revealed buyers converged on the luxury property sector like moths to a flame, with Miami house prices shooting beyond 44 per cent to $1.205 million in a year and Mermaid Waters house prices rising by 41.9 per cent to $1.22 million.

In neighbouring Mermaid Beach, a colossal 32.4 per cent hike sent house prices to a record $2.075 million.

But while the voracious growth decimated stock levels and burst the seaside dream for thousands of buyers hoping to bag a bargain by the beach, Ray White Surfers Paradise Group chief executive Andrew Bell says, after almost FEATURE STORY 24 months of price hikes the fever was breaking.

“Twenty months ago, you couldn’t have imagined the prices we’d achieve. This is the greatest boom in the history of the country … and the last thing I can remember that was close to this was 1988 and ’99 after the stock market crashed,” Bell says.

“People pulled their money out of shares and ploughed it back into real estate but it was short-lived. This boom is even stronger.

The difference now is the cheap money. People are more cavalier with it and it’s so affordable.

“But all markets, whether it’s gold or oil, go through cycles and property is so aligned to the economic cycle. So, we were due for a boom … and if you follow the cycles, two years of a boom market is about as long as they last.

“Now there are signals out there showing the brakes are being applied, whether that’s the regulations for borrowing [announced on November 1], chats about interest rates rising and then affordability being tested. You get half a dozen of those things like this and it’s like putting an anchor out.”

While the anchor might have been dropped, the city has moved up the search rankings to top place for overseas buyers, according to PropTrack’s Overseas Search Data Report released last month, with units in Surfers Paradise topping the national list for sales value, according to figures found in the Domain House Price Report.

The mass return of expats could also see the anchor lifted early next year, with the city’s annual auction – called The Event – tipped to be the best yet for the Ray White Surfers Paradise Group when it kicks off on January 23 at RACV Royal Pines Resort in Benowa.

Looking back over the past year, prestige property specialist Michael Kollosche, of real estate agency Kollosche, says the depth of the market was astonishing and had resulted in the firm collecting just over $230 million in unconditional sales in October alone.

The team also achieved a handful of jawdropping sales, such as 159 Hedges Avenue, Mermaid Beach, which recently fetched $15.75 million.

“There have been a lot of sales in that $10 million to $16 million range this year and a large portion of them were to locals with a few coming out of Sydney and Melbourne,” Kollosche says.

“I sold a block of land alone [900 square metres] at 139-141 Hedges Avenue for $17.5 million [in August]. I think the market will remain reasonably stable over the next 12 months because the Gold Coast is wellpositioned with the [Brisbane 2032 Olympics] and there’s a lot of infrastructure spending.”

For the team at Amir Prestige Property Agents, the year has been equally fruitful, after principal and director Amir Mian collected a suburb-record-smashing $23.75 million for the spectacular 5 McMillan Court, Southport, in March this year.

The sale came hot on the heels of yet another record-breaking sale for the firm at 187-191 Hedges Avenue, which achieved $22.5 million in the latter half of last year.

“The Gold Coast is poised for a pretty good decade between now and the Olympics … and I think it’s to do with the number of buyers who want clean air, a nice environment and a nice backyard,” Mian says. “A highlight sale for us was 41-45 The Promenade, Isle of Capri, which sold for $26.998 million … all our top sales were pretty much suburb record breakers.

“People are more than just getting caught in the Gold Coast movement – they are putting their kids in school here, and they are changing their jobs to live here.”

HEADLINE: A celbration of curves
TEXT:
A seven-year renovation has transformed the rundown Cove House into a stunning waterside oasis. By KATE FARRELLY Sometimes you stumble upon a home you didn’t even realise you were looking for.

So it was for Shane Noble in 2014.

He was hunting for a knock-down-rebuild project in Gunnamatta Bay but instead, at his daughter’s urging, he found himself on the threshold of Cove House, arguably Cronulla’s most iconic home.

“It was in a bad state of disrepair,” Noble says.

“But my daughter pestered me to come and have a look, and when we walked through the door we were absolutely sold.”

Completed in 1973 to a design by architect Reuben Lane, Cove House is a bold exercise in non-linear architecture. Curves now dominate both inside and out following the Nobles’ sympathetic renovation and restoration.

“It’s so impressive on first viewing because you have these very large, double-storey windows that front this large, circular lounge room,” Noble says. “It’s really the organic shapes within the house that are the selling point.”

The views are also key to the home’s appeal.

Sitting on a 1334-square-metre waterfront block with an expansive outlook over Port Hacking to Bundeena and the Royal National Park, the eye-catching residence has direct access to Salmon Haul Bay.

“There’s always something going on, a little bit of theatre on the waterway because we’re right at the entry to Port Hacking,” Noble says. “We regularly see dolphins, and last year we had a whale with her calf just outside the house.”

Noble’s favourite spaces in the home include DREAM HOMES an intimate study and the huge main bedroom, where a timber-clad Agape bath almost steals the show.

“Just before we bought the house we were staying in a magnificent hotel on the Italian lakes and we took inspiration from that,” he says. “We can lie in bed … and we can see all the views but no one can actually see inside the house. That’s the magic of the original design: it has fantastic sight lines with absolute privacy.”

Noble gives credit to interior architect Brendan Wong for refining the floor plan to be both beautiful and practical, with textured and finely patterned finishes adding another layer of interest to an already impressive property.

The seven-year transformation included a complete makeover of the front and back gardens, with landscape architects Secret Gardens given plenty of freedom to create an al fresco oasis.

A glass-fronted, mosaic-tiled pool is tucked under the house and adjoins striking, tiered gardens that continue the curved theme and include an oceanfront fire pit with seating.

“The house gives us joy every day,” Noble says.

“Good architecture is meant to make you feel good and this house does that.”

HEADLINE: Editor's Letter
TEXT: The beach, the sand, the ocean has a hold on everyone. For me, it’s a sweet reminder of home, strolling along the shores of Bar Beach on the NSW North Coast – a notion I didn’t know was so special to me until I moved to a place where the closest beach was a 2.5-hour drive away. Now in Sydney, my appreciation runs deep yet the faint smell of salty air still catches me by pleasant surprise. We live in a country that flexes arguably some of the best waterfront properties in the world. In this final edition of Prestige for 2021, we showcase the cream of the crop that’s on the market, from our Cronulla cover property with magical views across Salmon Haul Bay, an abode near Adelaide suspended high above the seascape with its own private beach, to a historic chapel along the “golden mile” of Sandy Bay, Tasmania. We’ll be back on January 26 and wish all our readers a safe and happy holiday

HEADLINE: ESG set to drive more upheaval in energy sector
TEXT:
M&A advisers in the energy sector are buckling in for a hectic ride in the new year, after 2021 was marked by a $100 billion-plus wave of deals and the shock exit of CEOs under huge pressure from the transition to low-carbon energy.

The frenzy of consolidation has thinned the pickings of corporate takeover targets at the big end of town and a repeat of that scale can hardly be expected. But ongoing deals such as the $42 billion merger between Woodside and BHP Petroleum, multiple transactions in the wings and assets on the block should ensure another action-packed year.

Driving much of the restructuring is the rise of environmental, social and governance (ESG) concerns, overwhelmingly focused on environmental. "It's interesting that it's taken the pandemic and ESG and oil price crashes and the like to galvanise some activity, but it's certainly been unprecedented," said Chris Forman, managing director at Rothschild, which is advising Senex Energy on the $900 million bid from Korea's Posco and advised Woodside on its deal to bring Global Infrastructure Partners into the Pluto-2 LNG expansion.

Mr Forman said ESG concerns were affecting oil and gas in multiple ways, not just the pursuit of scale to weather the transition behind Santos' $22 billion merger with Oil Search and the Woodside-BHP deal, to be overseen by new Woodside CEO Meg O'Neill.

Energy majors seeking to build capabilities in "new energy", pressure from investors to decarbonise their portfolios, and the recycling of assets into the hands of private operators that still have a mandate to invest in hydrocarbons were all drivers, said Mr Forman.

He now expects the ESG pressures to start filtering down to the smaller end of the sector. "Energy transition is an underlying theme that all organisations are focusing on," said Craig Rogers, energy M&A specialist at King & Wood Mallesons, which is advising Woodside on its BHP deal and worked for APA Group on its tilt at AusNet Services.

"For some it creates an opportunity, for some it's something that they need to deal with and something that they actively need to address. For others their existing business model is fundamentally changing, and for some it's opportunistic, it's about coming in and finding new areas and then being at the forefront.

"The theme is consistent, but the driver ... for each organisation depends upon where their existing business sits in that spectrum of transition."

Certainly, appetite from Korean and Japanese companies for Australian assets that can support the transition to low-carbon energy would continue for at least another 12 months, said Andrew Fiskin, head of DLA Piper's China practice in Australia.

The firm is advising Posco on its bid for east coast gas producer Senex Energy and was at the steel giant's side for its purchase of a stake in the Ravensthorpe nickel operation earlier in 2021.

"Large companies in these jurisdictions are positioning themselves for a lower carbon economy," Mr Fiskin said, pointing to the strategic drivers for both deals, the Senex one with "blue" hydrogen [gas-based with carbon capture] in mind, and Ravensthorpe as it relates to nickel for lithium-ion batteries.

Mr Fiskin said China was still keen on Australian energy, with early stage interest in renewables. But he expects Chinese bidders to hold off on any big moves until after the election, which should give "a bit more visibility on the approach that Australia's government will be taking to Chinese investment".

M&A activity in 2021 was also evident in electricity infrastructure, with Spark Infrastructure swallowed up by a group led by private equity giant Kohlberg Kravis Roberts for $5.2 billion, while Canada's Brookfield is poised to take AusNet Services in a $17.8 billion deal that trumps rival bidder APA.

In the renewables sector, 8 to 9 gigawatts of capacity changed hands in 2021, up from 2 to 3 GW in 2020, said David Dixon at Rystad Energy, who also noted the activity in retailing, where Shell snapped up green retailer Powershop.

Mr Dixon expects to see a steady preference among buyers for wind assets as utility PV suffers from low daytime prices as solar floods the system. Credit Suisse energy analyst Saul Kavonic expects the energy M&A wave to persist into 2022, spanning the fossil fuel, future-facing fuels and resources, decarbonisation technology and power distribution and mobility sectors.

"In 2022, we expect an expanded focus upon energy transformation opportunity sets, and portfolio rationalisation at legacy energy assets," Mr Kavonic said.

Energy transition targets could broaden beyond the establishment of operational footprints into niche capabilities and technologies across sectors such as retail demand management, e-mobility integration, hydrogen electrolyser and carbon abatement, he added.

Matt Rennie at consultancy Rennie Partners said Australia was entering the first of three significant five-year horizons that would see the energy market transform. For conventional coal power generators, it was critical the first big moves towards diversification occur in the next three years, he said, while cash flows remained relatively strong and before the next wave of renewable energy flooded into the market through Renewable Energy Zones.

"We expect to see increasing transactional activity from AGL, Origin Energy and EnergyAustralia as we move into horizon one, peaking in horizon two in the lead-up to 2030," Mr Rennie said.

He said the massive increase in grid-scale renewable capacity would create significant opportunities for regulated transmission networks. Distribution companies will begin to deploy capital expenditure later this decade to enable the penetration of distributed energy resources devices across rooftop solar, batteries and electric vehicles as the network becomes "bidirectional".

Among big electricity players, AGL, under chairman-turned CEO Graeme Hunt, will be on the front line as it heads towards its radical demerger, targeted by mid-2022. Infrastructure Capital Group (ICG), which in 2021 bought Meridian's Australian renewables plants among other acquisitions, expects to be equally busy in 2022, kicking off with a solar acquisition. It is also thought to be in the running for Elliott Green Power.

ICG executive director Edward Lloyd said the energy transition would drive the market for years to come. "It's not just about decarbonising and investing in renewable energy; it's how do we get to where we need to get to over a period of time," Mr Lloyd said.

That has seen ICG investing not just in wind and solar development opportunities but in TasGas Networks, which is pushing to get in on the hydrogen industry. Storage was also a sector "of great interest", Mr Lloyd said, signalling appetite for batteries and gas storage.

Carbon capture and storage (CCS) may also come onto the register for investment, particularly among parties in markets without geological opportunities for carbon storage, said Herbert Smiths Freehills partner Robert Merrick, adding that the commercial model for CCS was still developing.

"I still think 2022 will be a relatively busy year: I think the deals might be smaller, but possibly more of them," Mr Merrick said. "A lot of this has just been brought on by the dizzying array of possibilities that exist out there and different strategic approaches that have been taken to the energy transition, and how different people are approaching it."

Mr Merrick is watching who will take the oil and gas assets expected to be shed after consolidation among the larger players, pointing to a potential opening for private capital that has been less evident in Australian oil and gas than in North America and Europe. 'You'll also see private capital coming into the upstream ... That might come from private equity, family office-type money, and you might also see it come from some of the NOCs [national oil companies]," he said. "Those looking for energy security in Asia, particularly gas as a transition fuel, you might see more investment on that front."

Rystad's Jimmy Zeng is among those expecting that in oil and gas, Western Australia will be the focus of M&A, particularly the Perth Basin, which has emerged as a proven onshore gas province, with potential to supply LNG as well as the domestic market.

"Over the next five years, I would expect [the Perth Basin] would attract most of the M&A activity," Mr Zeng said.

Also outstanding in WA is a restructuring of the North West Shelf LNG venture, where Chevron has had its one-sixth stake on the block for 18 months but where a looming shortfall of gas reserves may deter buyers. Rothschild's Mr Forman said that gas issue would need to be resolved before any new entrant would buy in.

Selling oil and gas assets was a different game given the escalation of ESG priorities, he said. "The days of kind of just going out running a broad-brush auction and inviting all and sundry are probably over; you've got to be a bit smarter the way you go about the engagement process," he said. "Less capital is being allocated to hydrocarbons, that's just a fact, so it is a greater competition out there for the marginal equity dollar ... The universe of investors is certainly shrinking."

HEADLINE: Last mile tempers online shopper frenzy
TEXT:
Ruslan Kogan, the founder and chief executive of one of Australia's online retailing pioneers, Kogan.com, is convinced that by 2040, people will look back at the bump that e-commerce gained in the COVID-19 pandemic and view it as being relatively small.

But other big players in the retail sector, such as Wesfarmers chief executive Rob Scott, suspect that while online retail has made substantial headway since early in 2020, there is an innate desire among many shoppers for the full browsing and shopping experience, which can only come from being inside a bricks and mortar store.

Mr Scott is having an each-way bet. With the hardware giant Bunnings, discount department stores Kmart and Target, and the office supplies and stationery group Officeworks in the retail stable of Wesfarmers, he believes both traditional retail and e-commerce can grow.

Wesfarmers also has its own pure-play online retailer in catch.com.au, which is making rapid gains.

The tough lockdowns and restrictions in Sydney and Melbourne over several months supercharged the online channels for retailers by necessity. Click and collect gained in popularity as shoppers tired of the hefty delivery delays as Australia Post buckled under the strain.

Mr Scott said: "There's no doubt that we've had an artificial blip this year.

"Perhaps we've brought three years of online transferred into one."

But there is a real appetite from shoppers when the bricks and mortar outlets open again. That was noticeable when Sydney and Melbourne reopened.

"If I think of Bunnings and Kmart and Officeworks, customers love coming back into our stores," he said.

The arrival of the omicron strain has delivered fresh uncertainty and angst. Mr Kogan says the pandemic has supercharged the structural shift to online, but there's much more to go.

"There is no doubt that the pandemic caused more customers to learn about the benefits of online shopping and caused e-commerce penetration to accelerate," he said.

"However, if we were to fast-forward 20 years and take a look at a historical graph of Australia's e-commerce penetration, the COVID period will be an irrelevant little bump."

Mr Kogan believes Australia's e-commerce sector is "significantly under penetrated compared to many other developed markets".

The retail analysts from Barrenjoey Partners - Peter Marks, Tom Kierath and Ary Norozi - are closely scrutinising the landscape.

"COVID has undoubtedly accelerated the adoption of online shopping as consumers sought to minimise potential exposure to the virus and retailers were instructed by governments to close physical stores at various stages," they said.

Australian Bureau of Statistics data show that for the 12 months ended October 2021, online retail accounted for 11 per cent of Australian retail sales, up from 6 per cent for the 12 months ended February 2020, before the pandemic started.

The Barrenjoey analysts believe the online spike will not be as pronounced in 2022.

"As restrictions are eased and the economy reopens, we expect some moderation in the growth of online trading, but expect it will remain structurally higher as a proportion of retail sales," they said.

"Consumers have adopted new shopping behaviours and retailers continue to invest in improving their online offer."

Stockbroking research house MST Marquee in September predicted mature retailers in Australia were likely to close as many new stores as they opened over the next decade, leading to no net new store growth in bricks and mortar.

In non-food categories, online penetration is expected to reach 30 per cent in 10 years, up from 21 per cent. Bunnings' online share of sales was 2 per cent last year, compared with 11 per cent for US home improvement chains Lowes, and 17 per cent for Home Depot.

Mr Kogan said it was not just about a simple retail transaction either.

"The shift to e-commerce is a multi-generation paradigm shift to how we shop and obtain information," he said.

The avalanche of new customers migrating online has brought fresh headaches though for what is termed the "last mile" - households getting the goods into their hands in a timely manner and as efficiently as possible.

Mr Kogan accepts that logistics "has been and always will be one of the biggest challenges to online retailers".

"The best online retailers understand that customers want things fast, and have been making investments in achieving that for over a decade," he said.

It is a relentless uphill battle.

Customers are continually lifting their sights.

"When it comes to logistics and fast delivery, online shoppers have very high standards and will continue to raise their expectations," Mr Kogan said.

The Barrenjoey Partners analysts refer to Amazon founder Jeff Bezos and his view that online players need to continually lift the bar to meet "the ever-increasing expectations of 'divinely discontent' customers". Shipping times and costs are an important consideration for online shoppers, they say.

Kogan.com has just set up a new "last-mile" Kogan Delivery Services arm, which it is expanding after testing it in Melbourne, Sydney and Brisbane.

It will supplement the Australia Post deliveries which Kogan.com will still use, but marks the first time the e-tailer has opted for a do-it-yourself approach.

It is also establishing a similar in-house delivery service in New Zealand, where it owns the Mighty Ape online business. That NZ delivery business will be known as Jungle Express.

Mr Kogan said Kogan Delivery Services was providing "incredible benefits" and by mid this month had completed more than 100,000 deliveries.

Retailers across the board in physical stores and online are also grappling with shipping delays and supply chain disruptions in the pandemic.

Mr Kogan said: "I've been in this game for nearly 16 years, and I can say for that entire period there has never been a time of no disruptions.

"There's always a few curve balls being thrown at you at all times and that's what makes it such an exciting space in which to operate."

The adrenalin is always pumping and the company thrives on being able to find a solution.

Ordering more goods to be on the safe side brought Kogan.com some trouble, as excess inventory issues dragged down full-year profits. But having items out of stock is anathema to any retailer.

HEADLINE: The new financial networks taking it to the banks
TEXT:
DeFi The structure based on blockchain is pushing new frontiers.

It's almost 11pm on a drizzly night in mid-December and the underground bar of the Prince of York in the Sydney CBD is going off. A member of the Flight Facilities DJs is spinning tunes on an interior balcony as a bevy of well-dressed entrepreneurs groove and gossip with venture capital investors.

The Blockies after-party is in full swing. Drinks have been shouted by Mycelium, a Brisbane-based group that took out one of the major awards - start-up of the year - earlier in the evening at a ceremony organised by industry group Blockchain Australia to recognise leaders in the emerging crypto economy.

Mycelium operates in a mysterious sub-sector of crypto known as decentralised finance - "DeFi" - where activity has ballooned this year. Core functions of the banking system - including lending, borrowing, investing and trading derivatives - are being replicated in this digital shadow economy. The area is unregulated, but perhaps not for much longer.

Amid the hype and new jargon, AFR Weekend spent time with several Australian-based DeFi developers in December, to better understand the changes hurtling towards the financial system if decentralised technologies are adopted more broadly.

Given its fringe appeal and tiny scale at present, it's appropriate this Blockies shindig is taking place in an underground venue. But in a few hours, this posse will emerge from the basement bar and spill onto York Street.

Whether that is an apt metaphor for DeFi itself will depend on whether the movement can provide consumers and regulators with a better way of delivering financial services.

It's important first to grasp some foundational concepts in an area that is confusing for outsiders.

Decentralised finance refers to financial applications that run on blockchain technology, such as Ethereum, which can be thought of as a universally accessible global computer. Blockchain creates a record of transactions, duplicated across a network rather than being controlled centrally.

DeFi is creating bank-like functions, including borrowing and lending, that can be accessed by anyone connected to the internet. Traditional banks and brokers are not required.

Instead, the financial services are managed by computer protocols, known as "smart contracts". Like escrow accounts, these create and manage the financial contracts underpinning the services. They allow users to remain anonymous.

DeFi has also been made possible by the creation of "stablecoins". While their value is pegged to a real-world currency such as the US dollar, these stablecoins are created by private technology players to allow funds to move around the DeFi ecosystem, so users don't have to transfer in and out of fiat money every time they transact. Stablecoins can be purchased with money, or other cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin; markets are global and liquidity is deep.

A core principle is transparency. While the identity of those transacting remains anonymous, the public blockchain ledger means transactions can be seen by anyone who knows how to read them. This makes the system audible and fees transparent.

DeFi is creating an alternative global settlement layer for financial transactions that is standard and fast - transactions can be cleared in seconds, compared to days for much of traditional finance.

For now, DeFi is mostly self-contained inside the crypto economy, which exploded this year. The market capitalisation of DeFi protocols was $US166 billion ($230 billion) on Christmas Eve, according to CoinMarketCap. The total amount "locked" into DeFi loans was $US101 billion, according to DeFi Pulse, another crypto information source.

These amounts are minuscule compared to mainstream banking: Commonwealth Bank alone has $760 billion of deposits. The total market cap of all cryptocurrencies including bitcoin is $US2.4 trillion, or around a third of the value of the Australian property market.

It's early days. But in time, DeFi proponents expect it to not only power gaming, the metaverse and NFT [non-fungible token] markets, but also connect into parts of mainstream finance. Regulated banks might use DeFi infrastructure to provide new products or networks.

The digitisation of real-world assets, a process known as "tokenisation", could also lead to more assets traded using DeFi systems - complementing, or competing with, traditional financial activity.

DeFi began to take off mid-way through last year, as the price of bitcoin started to run, from $2000 at the start of 2019 to about $15,000 mid last year and about $70,000 on Christmas Eve. DeFi allows bitcoin investors to earn a return on their holdings and to borrow against it. The leverage allows investors to buy other crypto assets, or even property in the real world as stablecoins are transferred to national currencies via hundreds of crypto exchanges.

Commercial banks, governments and central banks are scrambling to understand these new dynamics. While the movement is attracting speculators bidding on wild price volatility, it could also represent the early stages of a new and more powerful internet, one that not only moves information but value. DeFi is building new systems to move money and to allow communities to self-govern. New internet-native business models are emerging, in a development known as Web3.

It's the morning after the Blockies after-party, December 10, and I'm talking to Sidney Powell, who is in New York, via Zoom.

Powell spent three years at National Australia Bank and is now running Maple Finance, a decentralised institutional capital marketplace.

Since international borders re-opened Powell, who is based in Sydney, has been travelling the globe relentlessly. He's speaking to AFR Weekend ahead of a presentation to an event known as DeFi Con 2021, which will be held in Brooklyn. In November, he was in Europe, at a gathering called Solana Breakpoint in Portugal.

"There is a lot of enthusiasm for the space, and I am seeing a lot of fresh faces coming across from TradFi [traditional finance] looking to build new start-ups," he says. "At Solana, I saw lots of people from investment banking, hedge funds and investments - from the heavy hitter financial space - excited enough to leave their high-paid jobs and take on the risk of founding a start-up."

Maple's opportunity has been created by banks' reluctance to lend to players in the crypto economy. (The phenomenon is known as "debanking" and is being investigated in 2022 by the Council of Financial Regulators.)

It also shows the power of stablecoins, which allow holders to earn a return. Institutional investors can pledge into the Maple platform USDC, the second-largest US dollar stablecoin. USDC has a market cap of $US40 billion and was created by Circle, a start-up backed by Visa and Coinbase, a crypto exchange that listed in January on the New York Stock Exchange.

Like an institutional banking desk, Maple then lends the USDC out. It is currently managing 66 active loans.

The core customer is a market-maker or arbitrageur providing liquidity on crypto exchanges. Maple does not lend to provide leverage on directional investment plays in crypto markets. "We have tried to be quite conservative from a risk perspective," Powell says.

The amount pledged by investors (known by the metric "total value locked" or TVL) across four Maple lending pools is around $500 million, having started at $17 million in May. Lenders have received interest (paid in USDC) of $5.1 million.

While traditional lenders have loans assessed by internal credit teams, Maple outsources this to teams of "pool delegates", who are vetted by Maple and who will be approved by the Maple community as its governance process matures.

Like a roaming team of underwriters, members are sophisticated credit analysts. They earn a fee of around 10 per cent of the interest paid by borrowers. Interest rates are bilaterally negotiated for each loan, based on supply and demand and company-specific risks for each loan.

Maple's borrowing rates are clearing at 10 per cent to 12 per cent annual percentage yield, with around 80 per cent of that passed through to investors.

Maple supported the first syndicated debt deal in DeFi in November. The borrower, Alameda Research, will use the USDC to provide liquidity to crypto exchanges as a market-maker. One of the largest crypto market trading firms, Alameda will borrow up to $1 billion over 12 months from a pool of stablecoin funds deposited by five investors.

"Funding for market-makers is something that banks would do for large trading houses like Optiver or Citadel, and if you were market-making in traditional instruments like EFTs or derivatives or commodities, you would be able to get a funding line from a bank for that," Powell says.

"But because [Alameda] are doing it in crypto, even though this is a very legitimate business operation, banks won't fund that - so we step in to provide that institutional finance layer."

In the future, Maple could expand lending for real-world assets, including data mining data centres used to verify blockchain transactions. These operations can generate a predictable yield, making it suitable for debt finance.

Another future business could involve lending to "decentralised autonomous organisations" (DAOs). These are a new model of corporate governance allowing communities to make decisions about a business operation via voting mechanisms embedded into blockchain technology.

"I think you will see loans to DAOs, or DAOs as [DeFi] borrowers, in 2022," Powell says.

While Maple Finance provides institutional services, DeFi has also taken off this year in retail markets.

Decentralised lending protocols such as Maker, Compound and Aave allow loans to be taken out anonymously, using cryptocurrencies as collateral. To reduce the risk of borrowers defaulting, they are required to over-collateralise.

A DeFi loan works like this: let's say you want to buy a $10,000 bike. You have 1/4 of a bitcoin (worth $17,000) but you don't want to sell it. The bitcoin can be "wrapped" into a smart contract and the collateral used to pull down a loan in a stablecoin, which can be moved to a crypto exchange and turned into cash. The loan can be paid back anytime, and the user pays the pre-determined interest rate to keep it open. When the loan is repaid with interest the bitcoin is unlocked and goes back to its owner, who now has a new bike.

What makes it different to a bank is an "oracle" is watching the price of the collateral: if the price of the crypto pledged as security drops below a pre-determined ratio, the smart contract liquidates the position automatically. Because of the threat of being liquidated, borrowers pledge much more - perhaps twice as much - crypto, which is taken out in dollars to provide a buffer if crypto prices fall.

It's this over-collateralisation that allows the financial contracts to be created between people who don't know each other and without a traditional intermediary like a bank or a broker standing in the middle. Crypto winnings can be spent in the real economy.

The top three lending protocols by value locked are Maker (TVL around $US19 billion as of Christmas Eve), Aave ($US12 billion), and Compound ($US12 billion).

Interest rates are determined algorithmically, depending on the demand for and supply of stablecoins, and have varied over the year from 3.5 per cent to 40 per cent when the market is severely constrained. Compound returned a variable annual percentage yield (APY) for supplying Dai (a popular stablecoin) that fluctuated between 2.83 per cent and 5.39 per cent this year, according Coinbase.

That's better than returns in banks or bond markets, although DeFi participants have no consumer protections, while also being exposed to the risk of smart contracts not working properly, or to fraud. Despite the risks, investors are flocking to a variety of crypto savings products, offering to beat bank saving rates, which are near zero. Crypto.com, Celsius and Nexo are the biggest global apps offering to put crypto to work. Crypto.com offers 8.5 per cent on bitcoin and 14 per cent on USDC.

In Australia, dozens of similar offerings are being developed, including from Finder, the comparison website and money app valued at $770 million, and the start-up Tiiink.

The week after my conversation with Sidney Powell, I'm eating yum cha with some of the leaders of Mycelium. It is December 14, five days since the Brisbane-based team won that start-up of the year award at the Blockies.

We are at the Palace Chinese restaurant in Sydney's Piccadilly Centre and the re-emergence of the coronavirus is not dampening this lunchtime crowd. Over baskets of steamed dumplings, roasted pork, fresh greens and a Tsingtao beer, the conversation delves deep into the challenges for DeFi next year.

Earlier this year Mycelium - whose founders were mates from the University of Queensland - launched Tracer DAO, a platform to trade perpetual swaps, allowing new, low-cost derivatives markets to be created. Next, it is creating the Reputation DAO, which co-founder Pat McNab says will help DeFi expand its offering by creating bridges to the traditional financial system.

He explains that in DeFi, reputation is subjective. Borrowers don't have an ability to provide the equivalent of a credit score to prove their capacity to repay. There's also a need to audit whether the "oracle" data services can be relied on. By establishing reputation, borrowers should be able to reduce the amount of collateral pledged to support loans.

"A standard reputation and credit layer will then openly assess DAOs and individuals in order to ultimately enable more rapid and higher-leverage lending and credit tools that closed-off institutions and credit networks will not be able to compete with," McNab explains.

As the food is cleared, conversation broadens to some major problems for incumbent bank and financial markets technology, including the creation of walled gardens, involving propriety products built on closed and ageing IT systems.

This means developers have to learn particular systems and languages, limiting the talent pool from which to recruit. Meanwhile, regulators and broader market participants struggle to assess risk. In contrast, DeFi offers a global, universal, development language - Solidity, the language of Ethereum - while the blockchain ledger is transparent for everyone to see.

"Right now the current digital financial system speaks many different digital languages with many separate computer networks that are relatively non-standardised," McNab told me. "This is an incredibly inefficient system, where risk is hard to measure and markets operate in silos.

"How we evolve this system is by building financial applications on top of blockchains, where all parties are operating on a single ledger in the same network of liquidity and capital," McNab says.

He points to applications that programmatically aggregate global interest rates and allocate their capital in the highest-returning parts of the digital economy. "These are applications that simply couldn't exist within the current financial system, which will only continue to become more efficient and divert interest from existing financial markets unless they adopt an open capital model."

The regulation of DeFi has been one of the hottest topics in global central bank and regulatory circles this year. Much of 2022 will be spent assessing a multitude of risks. Before DeFi is more broadly adopted, it will need to be properly regulated - something that was looking increasingly likely as 2021 drew to a close.

Despite the novel risks, the government in Australia is adopting crypto regulation including the formal recognition of DAOs in the Corporations Act. A report by EY in December pointed to the size of the prize: employment in the crypto sector, currently 11,600, could increase to over 200,000 workers by 2030, with the current $2 billion in economic activity soaring to $68 billion over the same timeframe.

Regulators will oversee new risks. One is the "rug pull", a new form of market manipulation where a scammer creates a token, lists it on a decentralised exchange but withdraws the holding from the liquidity pool to cause the price to fall to zero.

There have also been raids on oracle data price feeds, which tell smart contracts when the value of a security has fallen too low to back a loan, allowing assets pledged as security to be drained out. Meanwhile, anonymity creates problems around "know your client" (KYC) and "anti money laundering" (AML) compliance, raising the prospect of money-laundering and other illicit use of funds.

The decentralised autonomous organisation is not necessarily the best equipped to manage governance for emerging Web3 business models. Moresh Kokane, an Australian working with OpenDAO, a protocol for minting stablecoins, says DAOs are often dysfunctional.

"Just because we now use a new technology to interact with each other - the blockchain - does not mean that the human foibles of tribalism, venalism and often times outright corruption and subterfuge disappear," Kokane says. "Most DAOs struggle to overcome apathy from participants and the key decisions remain in the hands of the core groups."

The Bank of International Settlements said in a December report that DeFi's vulnerabilities "are severe, because of high leverage, liquidity mismatches, built-in interconnectedness and the lack of shock-absorbing capacity".

BIS, a global group of central banks, also questioned whether true decentralisation of power can be achieved. There is a "decentralisation illusion" in DeFi, it suggested, "since the need for governance makes some level of centralisation inevitable and structural aspects of the system lead to a concentration of power".

Someone thinking deeply of the regulatory challenges for DeFi - but who is optimistic they can be dealt with effectively - is Greg Medcraft, former chairman of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission. After a stint leading fintech policy at the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development in Paris, he returned to Australia mid-year, and the week before Christmas was elected as a board member of the new Digital Finance CRC, which is backed by the Reserve Bank.

Regulators in 2022 will be guided by the core principles of their mandates, he says. For example, securities regulators will want to ensure markets are fair, orderly and transparent and investors have trust and confidence.

Global co-ordination and standards for DeFi are critical. Medcraft suggests a "responsible person" should be accountable for protocol development, and regulatory "access points" need to be created, along with legal clarity for DAOs around the liability of governance token holders.

But once these are defined, Medcraft tells AFR Weekend he's optimistic DeFi could emerge with a technology and governance system that can enhance the financial system.

"Once a global regulatory framework exists for DeFi, I expect it to boom for real-world assets, redefining financial infrastructure and the role of intermediaries, to be more trusted advisers and custodians," he says.

"We are certainly on the edge of a revolution in financial services. Any repeatable and verifiable function can be replaced by smart contracts and AI."
